meta.title: Fine-tuning LLMs: The Complete Guide
meta.subtitle: Understanding how models learn - from pre-training to fine-tuning

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:pre-training:Pre-training} is teaching a {term:model:model} the fundamental patterns of language using MASSIVE amounts of unlabeled text (trillions of {term:token:tokens}). The {term:model:model} learns grammar, syntax, semantics, facts, and reasoning patterns - WITHOUT any human-labeled examples! It's like a child learning to speak by listening to millions of conversations.

The process of initializing {term:weights:model parameters} by training on a self-supervised objective (next token prediction or masked token prediction) over a large corpus. The {term:model:model} learns P(token|context) from the statistical patterns in text.

sections.title: Real Scale
sections.content:
• GPT-3: ~300 billion tokens (~570 GB of text)
  • LLaMA-2: ~2 trillion tokens
  • GPT-4: Unknown (estimated 10+ trillion)
  • Compute cost: $1M - $100M+
  • Time: Weeks on 1000s of GPUs

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:fine-tuning:Fine-tuning} takes a {term:pre-training:pre-trained} {term:model:model} that already 'knows' language and adapts it for YOUR specific task using YOUR {term:data:labeled data}. Instead of training billions of {term:weights:parameters} from random values, you start from a {term:model:model} that already understands language! This is {term:transfer-learning:transfer learning}.

Continuing training from {term:pre-training:pre-trained} {term:weights:weights} θ_pretrained on a task-specific dataset. The {term:model:model} adapts its representations while preserving general language knowledge. Can be full (all parameters) or partial (selected layers).

sections.title: Cost Comparison
sections.content:
Training from scratch:
  • Data: Trillions of tokens
  • Cost: ~$4.6M (GPT-3 scale)
  • Time: Weeks on 1000s of GPUs
Fine-tuning:
  • Data: 1K - 100K examples
  • Cost: ~$100 - $10K
  • Time: Hours on 1-8 GPUs
100x - 1000x cheaper!

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:encoder-only:Encoder-only} models like BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT use bidirectional attention - each {term:token:token} can see ALL other tokens (past AND future). This makes them excellent for understanding tasks (classification, NER) but unsuitable for text generation.

The attention mechanism has no causal mask, allowing position i to attend to all positions j ∈ [0, n]. Pre-trained using Masked Language Modeling ({term:mlm:MLM}) where 15% of tokens are masked and predicted using bidirectional context.

sections.title: BERT Attention Pattern
sections.content:
For sequence [CLS] The cat sat [SEP]:

Each token can attend to ALL other tokens (bidirectional):
  • [CLS] sees: [CLS], The, cat, sat, [SEP]
  • The sees: [CLS], The, cat, sat, [SEP]
  • cat sees: [CLS], The, cat, sat, [SEP]
Result: Every token has FULL context from both directions!

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:decoder-only:Decoder-only} models like GPT, LLaMA, and Mistral use causal (autoregressive) attention - each {term:token:token} can ONLY see previous tokens and itself (NOT future tokens). This enables text generation one {term:token:token} at a time.

Uses {term:causal-mask:causal masking} to prevent future token access. Pre-trained using next token prediction: P(t_i | t_1, ..., t_{i-1}). The {term:causal-mask:causal mask} is a lower triangular matrix applied to attention scores.

sections.title: GPT Attention Pattern
sections.content:
For sequence [BOS] The cat sat:

Each token can only see itself and PREVIOUS tokens:
  • [BOS] sees: only [BOS]
  • The sees: [BOS], The
  • cat sees: [BOS], The, cat
  • sat sees: [BOS], The, cat, sat
Result: Can't peek at future tokens!

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:mlm:MLM} is BERT's {term:pre-training:pre-training} objective. Randomly mask 15% of {term:token:tokens} and have the {term:model:model} predict the original ones using bidirectional context. It's like a fill-in-the-blank game - 'The [MASK] sat on the mat' → predict 'cat'.

Of the 15% selected tokens: 80% replaced with [MASK], 10% with random token, 10% unchanged. This prevents the model from only learning when [MASK] is present. Loss is computed only on masked positions.

sections.title: MLM in Action
sections.content:
Original sentence: "The cat sat on the mat"

Step 1: Select 15% of tokens → "cat", "mat"

Step 2: Transform selected tokens:
  • "cat" → [MASK] (80% chance)
  • "mat" → "dog" (10% random replacement)
Step 3: Model input: "The [MASK] sat on the dog"

Step 4: Model predicts:
  • Position 2: P("cat") = 0.89
  • Position 6: P("mat") = 0.72
Step 5: Loss computed only on masked positions!

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: The {term:cls-token:[CLS]} token is a special token prepended to every BERT input. Its final hidden state is designed to capture the 'summary' of the entire sequence through bidirectional attention. For classification tasks, you attach a classification head on TOP of this {term:cls-token:[CLS]} embedding.

The hidden state at position 0 after all transformer layers. Since BERT uses bidirectional attention, {term:cls-token:[CLS]} attends to ALL tokens and learns an aggregate representation during {term:pre-training:pre-training} (via NSP task) and {term:fine-tuning:fine-tuning}.

sections.title: Using [CLS] for Classification
sections.content:
Input: [CLS] I love this movie! [SEP]

Step 1: Pass through BERT (12 layers)
  • hidden_states shape: (batch, 7, 768)
Step 2: Extract [CLS] embedding
  • cls_embed = hidden_states[:, 0, :]
  • shape: (batch, 768)
Step 3: Add classification head
  • logits = Linear(768, 2)(cls_embed)
Step 4: Apply softmax → [0.08, 0.92] → Positive!

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: The {term:causal-mask:causal mask} prevents each position from 'seeing' future {term:token:tokens}. Like reading a book with future pages covered - position 3 can see positions 1, 2, 3 but NOT 4, 5. Essential for autoregressive generation where we predict one {term:token:token} at a time.

An upper triangular matrix of -∞ values added to attention scores BEFORE {term:softmax:softmax}. Since exp(-∞) → 0, future positions get zero attention weight after softmax. Creates a lower triangular attention pattern.
sections.formula: Attention = {term:softmax:softmax}(QK^T / √d + Mask), where Mask[i,j] = 0 if j ≤ i, else −∞

sections.title: Mask Visualization (seq_len=4)
sections.content:
Before softmax (raw mask values):
t0 t1 t2 t3 t0 [ 0, -∞, -∞, -∞ ] t1 [ 0, 0, -∞, -∞ ] t2 [ 0, 0, 0, -∞ ] t3 [ 0, 0, 0, 0 ]

After softmax: Lower triangular matrix where each row sums to 1.0. Since exp(-∞) = 0, future tokens are completely ignored.

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: During training, instead of using the {term:model:model}'s own predictions as input for the next step, we use the actual correct {term:token:tokens} from the training {term:data:data}. This prevents error accumulation and enables PARALLEL processing of entire sequences in ONE forward pass!

At training time, input at position i is always the ground truth token t_i, NOT the model's prediction. Combined with {term:causal-mask:causal masking}, this allows computing {term:loss:loss} for ALL positions in ONE forward pass - making training fast.

sections.title: Training vs Inference
sections.content:
TRAINING (teacher forcing, parallel):
  • Input: [BOS, 'The', 'cat', 'sat']
  • Target: ['The', 'cat', 'sat', EOS]
  • ALL 4 predictions in 1 forward pass!
  • Loss computed at all positions simultaneously
INFERENCE (autoregressive, sequential):
  • Step 1: [BOS] → predict 'The'
  • Step 2: [BOS, 'The'] → predict 'cat'
  • Step 3: [BOS, 'The', 'cat'] → predict 'sat'
  • 3 separate forward passes - much slower!

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:bos-token:BOS} is a special {term:token:token} that marks where a sequence starts. It gives the {term:model:model} a consistent starting point for generation and helps distinguish between new conversations vs continuations.
A special token ID (often 1 or 2) prepended to input sequences. Has its own learned embedding vector signaling sequence start.

sections.title: Tokenization with BOS
sections.content:
Text: "Hello world"

Tokenized: [1, 15496, 995]
  • 1 = BOS token
  • 15496 = "Hello"
  • 995 = "world"

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:eos-token:EOS} marks where a sequence ends. During generation, when the {term:model:model} outputs {term:eos-token:EOS}, we stop generating. During training, it teaches the {term:model:model} when responses should end.
A special token ID appended to target sequences. The {term:model:model} learns to predict {term:eos-token:EOS} when the response should terminate.

sections.title: During Generation
sections.content:
Response tokens: [450, 7483, 338, 3681, 2]
  • Token IDs 450, 7483, 338, 3681 = response text
  • 2 = EOS token (signals stop)
Generation stops when: argmax(logits) == EOS_token_ID

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:sft:SFT} teaches the {term:model:model} to follow instructions using human-written (instruction, response) pairs. The {term:model:model} learns patterns like 'when given this instruction, respond this way'. It's still next-{term:token:token} prediction - just on curated {term:data:data}!

Same {term:loss:loss} function as {term:pre-training:pre-training}! The key difference is the {term:data:data} format (instruction-response pairs) and optional prompt masking (labels=-100 for prompt {term:token:tokens} so they don't contribute to {term:loss:loss}).

sections.title: SFT Data Format
sections.content:
JSONL format (industry standard):
{"messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are helpful."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Translate: Hello"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Bonjour"} ]}

Key point: Loss is computed only on assistant response tokens! Prompt tokens have labels = -100 (ignored by PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss).

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: The {term:attention-mask:attention mask} tells the {term:model:model} which {term:token:tokens} are real and which are just padding (added to make sequences equal length in a batch). Padding tokens should be ignored in attention calculations.

A binary mask where 1 = real token, 0 = padding. Applied to attention scores by setting padding positions to -∞ before {term:softmax:softmax}. Combined with {term:causal-mask:causal mask} in decoder-only {term:model:models}.
sections.formula: attention_mask[i] = 1 if token[i] is real, else 0

sections.title: Padding Example
sections.content:
Batch (padded to max length):
  • Seq 1: [BOS, The, cat, sat, EOS] → mask: [1,1,1,1,1]
  • Seq 2: [BOS, Hi, EOS, PAD, PAD] → mask: [1,1,1,0,0]
Result: PAD tokens don't affect other tokens' representations.

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:bce-loss:Binary Cross-Entropy} measures how wrong your {term:model:model}'s {term:probability:probability} prediction is for a YES/NO question. Think: confident + wrong = massive penalty!
Measures dissimilarity between predicted {term:probability:probability} p and true binary label y ∈ {0, 1}. The log function heavily penalizes confident wrong predictions.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Spam Detection:
  • True = spam (y=1), Prediction = 95% spam → Loss = −log(0.95) = 0.05 ✓
  • True = spam (y=1), Prediction = 5% spam → Loss = −log(0.05) = 3.0 ✗
Being confidently wrong is 60× worse!

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:cce-loss:Categorical Cross-Entropy} is for 'pick ONE out of many'. Only the true class's {term:probability:probability} matters for the {term:loss:loss}.
For K classes with one-hot targets, simplifies to negative log of the true class probability.

sections.title: Calculation Example
sections.content:
Image Classification (3 classes):
  • Classes: [cat, dog, bird]
  • True: dog → one-hot: [0, 1, 0]
  • Prediction: [0.1, 0.85, 0.05]
Loss: −log(0.85) = 0.16
Only the dog {term:probability:probability} (0.85) mattered!

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:mse-loss:MSE} measures 'how far off' your numeric prediction is. Big errors hurt quadratically more than small ones.
Average of squared differences between predicted ŷ and true y values.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
House Price Prediction:
  • True: $350K, Predicted: $320K
  • Error: $30K → Error²: $900M
Doubling the error → 4× the {term:loss:loss}!

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:sigmoid-activation:Sigmoid} squashes any number to (0, 1). Each output is INDEPENDENT - that's why it's used for {term:multi-label:multi-label} classification!
S-shaped function. Large positive → ~1, large negative → ~0, zero → exactly 0.5.

sections.title: Sigmoid vs Softmax
sections.content:
{term:softmax:Softmax}: [2.0, 1.0, 0.5] → [0.59, 0.24, 0.17] sum = 1.0

{term:sigmoid-activation:Sigmoid}: [2.0, 1.0, 0.5] → [0.88, 0.73, 0.62] each independent!

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:multi-class:Multi-class} = 'pick exactly ONE' from many options. Uses {term:softmax:Softmax} - {term:probability:probabilities} sum to 1, forcing a single choice.
Mutually exclusive classes. Output is a valid {term:probability:probability} distribution.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
• Image classification: cat/dog/bird (one per image)
  • Sentiment: positive/negative/neutral (one feeling)
  • Digit recognition: 0-9 (one digit)

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content:
{term:multi-label:Multi-label} asks MULTIPLE independent yes/no questions:
  • 'Is it a car?' → 95% yes
  • 'Is it red?' → 87% yes
  • 'Is it German?' → 12% no
Each answered separately!
Uses {term:sigmoid-activation:sigmoid} per label (independent outputs) and {term:bce-loss:BCE} per label.

sections.title: Movie Genre Example
sections.content:
Labels: [action, comedy, romance, horror]
Predictions: [0.92, 0.85, 0.15, 0.03]
Result: action AND comedy!

Multi-class would force ONE choice - wrong!

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content:
{term:token-classification:Token classification} assigns a label to EACH {term:token:token}:
John→PERSON, works→O, at→O, Google→ORG
Classification head applied to every {term:hidden-state:hidden state}, not just {term:cls-token:[CLS]}.

sections.title: Shape Comparison
sections.content:
• Regression: [batch, 1]
  • Classification: [batch, K]
  • Token Classification: [batch, seq_len, K]

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: The {term:lm-head:LM head} is the final layer: converts {term:hidden-state:hidden states} to next-{term:token:token} {term:logits:logits}. LLaMA-7B: 4096 → 32000 (vocab size)!
Linear projection from hidden dimension to {term:vocabulary:vocabulary} size.

sections.title: Standard vs Modified
sections.content:
Standard (generation): Hidden → LM Head → Vocab {term:logits:logits}

[ADVANCED] Modified (classification): Hidden → Replace LM Head → Custom Head (4096→3)

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: The {term:hidden-state:hidden state} is a {term:token:token}'s internal representation after transformer layers. Encodes meaning in context: 'bank' has different representations in 'river bank' vs 'money bank'!
Output vector at each position. Used by downstream heads for predictions.

sections.title: Common Dimensions
sections.content:
• BERT-base: 768
  • BERT-large: 1024
  • LLaMA-7B: 4096
  • LLaMA-70B: 8192

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:ner:NER} finds and classifies 'named things' in text: people, organizations, locations, dates.
A {term:token-classification:token classification} task using BIO tagging: B-TYPE (begin), I-TYPE (inside), O (outside).

sections.title: BIO Tagging Example
sections.content:
Elon → B-PER (Begin Person)
Musk → I-PER (Inside Person)
works → O (Outside)
at → O
Tesla → B-ORG (Begin Organization)

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:pos-tagging:POS tagging} labels each word with its grammatical role: noun, verb, adjective, etc.
A {term:token-classification:token classification} task with grammatical category labels. Common tagsets: Penn Treebank (45 tags), Universal Dependencies (17 tags).

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
The → DET (Determiner)
quick → ADJ (Adjective)
fox → NOUN
jumps → VERB

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:extractive-qa:Extractive QA} finds the answer WITHIN the passage. It doesn't generate - just highlights the span.
Predicts START and END positions. Each {term:token:token} gets two scores: 'is this the start?' and 'is this the end?'

sections.title: Span Prediction
sections.content:
Context: 'Paris is the capital of France'
Question: 'What is the capital?'
Prediction: Start=0, End=0 → 'Paris'

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: The {term:mask-token:[MASK]} token is BERT's 'fill in the blank'. Replace the word you want to predict with {term:mask-token:[MASK]}, the {term:model:model} predicts what should go there.
Special {term:token:token} (typically ID 103 in BERT). Output at this position is a {term:probability:distribution} over entire {term:vocabulary:vocabulary}.

sections.title: Fill-in-the-Blank
sections.content:
Input: 'The [MASK] of France is Paris'
Output:
  • capital: 0.85
  • city: 0.06
  • heart: 0.02

preference-data.title: Preference Data - Human Judgment in Data Form

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:preference-data:Preference data} captures human judgment: 'Response A is better than Response B for this prompt.' It's the fuel for training {term:reward-model:reward models} and direct preference optimization. Without it, we can't teach {term:model:models} what 'better' means to humans.

Pairs of (prompt, chosen_response, rejected_response). Used with Bradley-Terry model to train {term:reward-model:reward model}: R(chosen) > R(rejected). The {term:reward-model:reward model} then guides {term:policy:policy} optimization.

sections.title: How It's Collected
sections.content:
Step 1: Generate 4 responses to same prompt
Step 2: Human ranks: Response 3 > Response 1 > Response 2 > Response 4
Step 3: Create pairs:
(prompt, chosen=3, rejected=4) (prompt, chosen=3, rejected=2) (prompt, chosen=1, rejected=4) ...

Criteria: Helpfulness, harmlessness, honesty

system-prompt.title: System Prompt - The Model's Operating Instructions

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: The {term:system-prompt:system prompt} sets the stage for the entire conversation. It defines the {term:model:model}'s persona, capabilities, constraints, and behavior. Think of it as the 'job description' given to the {term:model:model} before any conversation begins.

Prepended to every conversation. Unlike user messages, system prompts are designed to persist and influence ALL subsequent responses. Typically marked with special {term:token:tokens} or placed in a reserved position in the {term:chat-template:chat template}.

sections.title: Example System Prompts
sections.content:
Simple:
You are a helpful assistant.

Complex:
You are a Python expert. Rules: 1. Always explain before coding 2. Use type hints 3. Never use deprecated APIs 4. If unsure, say so

Key: The {term:model:model} references this for EVERY response!

sections.title: Why It Exists
sections.content:
LLMs don't understand 'conversations' - they only see a flat sequence of {term:token:tokens}. The {term:chat-template:chat template} is the 'grammar' that converts structured messages (system, user, assistant) into a single string the {term:model:model} was TRAINED on.

Problem: You have: [{role: user, content: 'Hi'}]
Model needs: A specific token sequence like <|im_start|>user\nHi<|im_end|>

Without correct template: The model sees garbage and performance collapses!

A Jinja2 template stored in tokenizer.chat_template. The method tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages) processes the message list and outputs a tokenizable string with proper special {term:token:tokens} for role boundaries.

sections.title: Transformation: JSON → Tokens
sections.content:
Input (Python list of dicts):
[{"role": "system", "content": "Be helpful"}, {"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Hello!"}]

After apply_chat_template (ChatML format):
<|im_start|>system Be helpful<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user Hi<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant Hello!<|im_end|>

Then tokenized: [32001, 1587, 10, 1763, ...] → ready for model!

sections.title: Common Formats
sections.content:
ChatML (Mistral, Qwen, many OSS):
<|im_start|>{role} {content}<|im_end|>

LLaMA-2 Chat:
<s>[INST] <<SYS>> {system} <</SYS>> {user} [/INST] {assistant} </s>

Alpaca:
### Instruction: {input} ### Response: {output}

Golden rule: Use the template the model was trained with. Check tokenizer.chat_template!

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: A {term:reward-model:reward model} is a neural network trained to predict 'how much would a human like this response?' Given a prompt and response, it outputs a single number (the {term:reward:reward} score). It's the automated judge that enables RLHF at scale.

Trained on {term:preference-data:preference data} using Bradley-Terry pairwise ranking {term:loss:loss}. Input: (prompt, response). Output: scalar {term:reward:reward}. Often initialized from SFT {term:model:model} with a linear head added.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
Input 1: (prompt, 'Helpful detailed answer') → {term:reward:R} = 0.85
Input 2: (prompt, 'I don't know') → {term:reward:R} = 0.12
Input 3: (prompt, 'Harmful response') → {term:reward:R} = -0.94

Training: ~50K-100K preference pairs
Architecture: LLM backbone + Linear(hidden→1)

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: Transfer learning takes knowledge learned on one task (usually with massive {term:data:data}) and applies it to a different, related task. Instead of training from scratch, you 'transfer' what the {term:model:model} already knows. Like a chef who learned French cuisine can quickly adapt to Italian - the core skills transfer!

Initialize {term:model:model} with {term:pre-training:pre-trained} {term:weights:weights} instead of random values. Then {term:fine-tuning:fine-tune} on target task. The {term:pre-training:pre-trained} representations provide a strong starting point, requiring far less task-specific {term:data:data}.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
Without transfer learning:
Train from scratch → Need 1M examples, weeks of training

With transfer learning:
Start from pre-trained → Need 1K examples, hours of training

Why it works: Language understanding transfers across tasks!

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:full-finetuning:Full fine-tuning} updates ALL {term:weights:parameters} of the {term:model:model} - every single weight in every layer gets adjusted. It's like sending a student to a completely new school where everything they learned gets refined. Maximum flexibility but maximum cost.

All {term:weights:parameters} θ in the {term:model:model} are {term:trainable-layer:trainable} and updated via gradient descent. Nothing is {term:frozen-layer:frozen}. This allows the {term:model:model} to maximally adapt but requires storing full optimizer states for every parameter.

sections.title: Resource Comparison
sections.content:
LLaMA-7B Full Fine-tuning:
  • Trainable params: 7 billion (100%)
  • GPU VRAM needed: ~28 GB (FP16 weights) + ~56 GB (optimizer states)
  • Total: ~84 GB → Need 2-4 A100 GPUs
  • Storage per task: ~14 GB checkpoint
When to use: Large diverse dataset, high budget, maximum customization needed.

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:partial-finetuning:Partial fine-tuning} freezes some layers and only trains others. Think of it like a musician who's mastered scales (keep those frozen) but needs to learn a new song (train the output layers). You preserve foundational knowledge while adapting for the task.

Selected layers have {term:trainable-layer:requires_grad=True}, others are {term:frozen-layer:frozen} (requires_grad=False). Common patterns: freeze all but last N transformer blocks, or freeze embedding + early layers while training attention/FFN in later layers.

sections.title: Example Configuration
sections.content:
LLaMA-7B (32 layers):
  • Freeze layers 0-24 (embedding + first 25 transformer blocks)
  • Train layers 25-31 (last 7 blocks) + LM head
  • Trainable: ~1.5B params (21% of model)
  • VRAM saved: ~60% reduction vs full
Trade-off: Less expressive than full fine-tuning, but much cheaper.

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:peft:PEFT} is a family of techniques that achieve fine-tuning by training only a tiny fraction of parameters - often less than 1% - while keeping the original {term:model:model} completely {term:frozen-layer:frozen}. It's like adding sticky notes to a textbook instead of rewriting it.

Keep all pretrained {term:weights:weights} {term:frozen-layer:frozen}. Add small {term:trainable-layer:trainable} modules (adapters, low-rank matrices, or soft prompts). Only new parameters are updated. Original model is preserved completely.

sections.title: PEFT Methods
sections.content:
• {term:lora:LoRA}: Add low-rank matrices to attention layers
  • {term:prefix-tuning:Prefix Tuning}: Learnable vectors in K/V attention
  • {term:prompt-tuning:Prompt Tuning}: Learnable soft prompts before input
  • {term:adapter:Adapters}: Small neural networks inserted between layers
Benefit: Same base model, different adapters for different tasks!

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:lora:LoRA} is the most popular {term:peft:PEFT} technique. Instead of updating a huge weight matrix W (say 4096×4096 = 16M params), it learns two small matrices A and B whose product approximates the weight change. It's like finding a shortcut that captures 99% of the improvement with 1% of the parameters.

Example: Single attention layer (4096×4096):
  • Full: 16,777,216 params
  • LoRA (r=8): (4096×8) + (8×4096) = 65,536 params
  • Savings: 99.6% fewer parameters!
LLaMA-7B with LoRA:
  • Original: 7B params → ~4M trainable (0.06%)
  • Storage: 7B checkpoint → ~32 MB adapter

Implementation note: Matrix A is initialized with scaled random values (÷√r), Matrix B is initialized to zeros so ΔW starts at zero. This ensures the model starts exactly as pretrained.

sections.title: Parameter Savings
sections.content:
Example: Single attention layer (4096×4096):
  • Full: 16,777,216 params
  • LoRA (r=8): (4096×8) + (8×4096) = 65,536 params
  • Savings: 99.6% fewer parameters!
LLaMA-7B with LoRA:
  • Original: 7B params → ~4M trainable (0.06%)
  • Storage: 7B checkpoint → ~32 MB adapter

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: The rank {term:lora-rank:r} controls how 'expressive' the {term:lora:LoRA} adaptation can be. Higher rank = more capacity to learn complex changes, but more parameters. Lower rank = less capacity but cheaper. Think of it like choosing brush size when painting - bigger brush covers more but less precise.

Rank {term:lora-rank:r} is the inner dimension of the low-rank decomposition. For B ∈ ℝ^{d×r} and A ∈ ℝ^{r×k}, trainable parameters = r×(d+k). Based on the hypothesis that weight updates during fine-tuning have low 'intrinsic rank' - they can be expressed in a much smaller dimensional space.

sections.title: Choosing Rank
sections.content:
Guidelines:
  • r = 4-8: Simple tasks (style, basic classification)
  • r = 16-32: Standard fine-tuning, instruction following
  • r = 64-128: Complex domains (legal, medical, coding)
Experiment: Many studies show r=16 is often sufficient even for complex tasks. Increasing r beyond 16-32 yields diminishing returns.

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: The {term:lora-alpha:alpha} parameter controls how much the {term:lora:LoRA} adaptation 'contributes' to the output. Higher alpha = stronger adaptation effect. It's like a volume knob for the fine-tuning signal.

The scaling factor multiplies the LoRA update before adding to the frozen weight output. The effective scaling is {term:lora-alpha:α}/{term:lora-rank:r}. Common practice: set {term:lora-alpha:α} = 2×{term:lora-rank:r} or {term:lora-alpha:α} = {term:lora-rank:r}.

sections.title: Practical Settings
sections.content:
Common configurations:
  • r=8, α=16: Effective scale = 2.0 (stronger adaptation)
  • r=16, α=16: Effective scale = 1.0 (balanced)
  • r=32, α=16: Effective scale = 0.5 (subtle adaptation)
Rule of thumb: α = 2×r keeps consistent 'strength' regardless of rank choice.

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: A {term:frozen-layer:frozen} layer has its {term:weights:weights} fixed during training - {term:data:data} flows through it, but {term:gradient:gradients} don't update it. Like reading a textbook without highlighting - you use the knowledge but don't modify the book.

Set requires_grad=False on {term:weights:parameters}. The forward pass proceeds normally, but during backward pass, {term:gradient:gradients} are not computed for these {term:weights:weights}, and optimizer ignores them.
sections.formula: for param in frozen_layers: param.requires_grad = False

sections.title: Code Example
sections.content: for name, param in model.named_parameters(): if 'embed' in name or 'layers.0' in name: param.requires_grad = False # Frozen else: param.requires_grad = True # Trainable

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:trainable-layer:Trainable} layers have their {term:weights:weights} updated during training based on {term:gradient:gradients}. These are the layers that 'learn' and adapt to your specific task.

Layers with requires_grad=True. {term:gradient:Gradients} are computed during backward pass and optimizer updates these {term:weights:weights}. Memory for optimizer states (momentum, variance in AdamW) is allocated only for {term:trainable-layer:trainable} parameters.

sections.title: Memory Impact
sections.content:
AdamW optimizer per trainable parameter:
  • Momentum (1st moment): 4 bytes (FP32)
  • Variance (2nd moment): 4 bytes (FP32)
  • Optimizer states total: 8 bytes per param
Full training memory per param:
  • Weight: 2 bytes (FP16/BF16)
  • Gradient: 2-4 bytes
  • Optimizer states: 8 bytes
  • Total: ~12-14 bytes per trainable param
Fewer {term:trainable-layer:trainable} params = less VRAM!

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:prefix-tuning:Prefix tuning} adds learnable vectors to the Key and Value matrices of attention across multiple layers. It's like giving the {term:model:model} a 'learned context' that steers its attention without changing any original {term:weights:weights}.

Insert learnable prefix embeddings P_k, P_v into the Key and Value sequences at each transformer layer. Only prefix parameters are trained. The model learns what 'context' to provide that guides generation.

sections.title: Comparison
sections.content: More control than {term:prompt-tuning:prompt tuning} (affects all layers, not just input). Less popular than {term:lora:LoRA} because it changes attention patterns in complex ways. Good for generation tasks.

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:prompt-tuning:Prompt tuning} adds learnable 'soft prompt' embeddings at the INPUT layer only (before the first transformer block). These are continuous vectors that guide the frozen {term:model:model} toward the desired behavior.

Learn continuous embeddings [v₁, v₂, ..., vₙ] prepended to input embeddings. Only these soft prompt vectors are trained. The frozen {term:model:model} then processes [soft_prompt; input] as one sequence.

sections.title: Comparison
sections.content: Simplest {term:peft:PEFT} method. Fewest parameters (~10K-100K). Best for tasks close to pretraining distribution. Less effective for tasks requiring deep model adaptation.

sections.title: What It Does
sections.content: {term:adapter:Adapter} layers are small neural network modules inserted between transformer layers. They have a bottleneck architecture: project down to small dimension, apply nonlinearity, project back up. Like adding specialized filters to a camera lens.
Insert adapter module: h' = h + f(h×W_down)×W_up where W_down ∈ ℝ^{d×r}, W_up ∈ ℝ^{r×d}. The bottleneck dimension r is small (8-256). Adapters are placed after attention and/or FFN sublayers.

sections.title: Architecture
sections.content:
• Bottleneck: 768 → 64 → 768 (for BERT-base)
  • Adds ~2% extra params per layer
  • Can be swapped for different tasks
Predates LoRA but less popular now because LoRA is simpler and often more efficient.

slides.title: What Does It Mean to Train a Model?

content.title: The Core Idea
content.content: Training = adjusting the {term:model:model}'s {term:weights:parameters} (billions of numbers) so that it produces useful outputs. Like adjusting the knobs on a radio until you get clear sound - except there are billions of knobs!

content.title: What Does the Model Actually Learn?
content.content:
We don't know exactly what's stored in those billions of {term:weights:parameters}, but research suggests:

• Grammar & Syntax: Sentence structure, word order rules
• Semantics: Word meanings, relationships, synonyms
• World Knowledge: Facts about entities, events, history
• Reasoning Patterns: Logical inference, cause-effect relationships

The {term:model:model} learns from statistical patterns in the {term:data:data} - it sees 'Paris' following 'capital of France' millions of times!

The Training Loop (same for both!):
for batch in data: predictions = model(batch.input) # Forward pass loss = compute_loss(predictions, batch.target) # How wrong? gradients = loss.backward() # Which direction to improve? optimizer.step(gradients) # Update weights

content.title: {term:encoder-only:Encoder-only} Models = Understanding Machines
content.content: Models like BERT, RoBERTa, and sentence transformers use bidirectional attention. Each {term:token:token} sees ALL other {term:token:tokens} (past AND future). Great for understanding text, NOT for generating it.

content.title: {term:pre-training:Pre-training}: Masked Language Modeling ({term:mlm:MLM})
content.content:
The Game: Mask 15% of {term:token:tokens}, predict the originals!

Masking strategy (of the 15% selected):
  • 80% → [MASK] token
  • 10% → Random word ("dog", "blue", etc.)
  • 10% → Unchanged (prevents overfitting to [MASK])
Example:
  • Original: "The cat sat on the mat"
  • Input: "The [MASK] sat on the [MASK]"
  • Model predicts: "cat" (89% confident), "mat" (72% confident)

Also: Next Sentence Prediction (NSP)
Given sentence A, is sentence B the actual next sentence or a random one?
The {term:cls-token:[CLS]} token's output is used for this binary classification during {term:pre-training:pre-training}.

content.title: {term:fine-tuning:Fine-tuning}: Add a Head on Top
content.content:
For Classification:
  1. Input: [CLS] I love this movie! [SEP]
  2. Extract [CLS] embedding (768-dim vector)
  3. Add: Linear(768, num_classes)
  4. Output: [0.08, 0.92] → Positive!
For Token Classification (NER):
  1. Input: [CLS] John works at Google [SEP]
  2. Extract ALL token embeddings
  3. Add: Linear(768, num_labels) per token
  4. Output per token: ["O", "B-PER", "O", "O", "B-ORG"]
Alternative: Use pooled output (mean of all tokens) instead of just [CLS].

Key Insight: The {term:cls-token:[CLS]} token learns to aggregate sequence information through self-attention during {term:pre-training:pre-training} (via NSP). During {term:fine-tuning:fine-tuning}, backpropagation teaches it to aggregate information relevant to YOUR task.

content.title: {term:decoder-only:Decoder-only} Models = Generation Machines
content.content: Models like GPT, LLaMA, Mistral use causal (autoregressive) attention. Each {term:token:token} can ONLY see previous {term:token:tokens} - enabling generation one {term:token:token} at a time.

content.title: {term:pre-training:Pre-training}: Next Token Prediction
content.content:
The Objective: Given all previous {term:token:tokens}, predict the next one!

Example:
  • Input: "The capital of France is"
  • Target: "Paris"
Model outputs a probability distribution over the ENTIRE vocabulary (~50K tokens):
  • P("Paris") = 0.92
  • P("Lyon") = 0.03
  • P("the") = 0.01
  • ... 49,996 other tokens ...

content.title: How Labels Are Created (Auto-Shifted!)
content.content:
The Ground Truth is self-generated! Just shift input by 1 token:

Sequence: "The cat sat on mat"
  • Input: [BOS, The, cat, sat, on, mat]
  • Labels: [The, cat, sat, on, mat, EOS]
What each position predicts:
  • Position 0 (BOS) → predicts "The"
  • Position 1 (The) → predicts "cat"
  • Position 5 (mat) → predicts EOS (end!)
Important: HuggingFace's DataCollatorForLanguageModeling handles this shifting automatically! You just copy input_ids to labels.

Why {term:causal-mask:Causal Mask}?
Without it, position 3 could 'cheat' by looking at position 4 when predicting what comes after position 3. The mask adds -∞ to future positions → exp(-∞) = 0 after {term:softmax:softmax} → zero attention to future.

Step 1: Raw {term:data:Data}
  • Sentence 1: "The cat sat" (from a book)
  • Sentence 2: "Hello world" (from the web)

Step 2: Tokenize
  • Sentence 1: ["The", "cat", "sat"] → [464, 3797, 3332]
  • Sentence 2: ["Hello", "world"] → [15496, 995]
Vocabulary size: 50,257 (GPT-2)

Step 3: Add Special {term:token:Tokens} ({term:bos-token:BOS}, {term:eos-token:EOS})
  • Seq 1: [1, 464, 3797, 3332, 2] = [BOS, The, cat, sat, EOS]
  • Seq 2: [1, 15496, 995, 2] = [BOS, Hello, world, EOS]

Step 4: Pad to Same Length (LEFT Padding for Decoders)

Max length = 5, pad on LEFT for decoder models:
  • Seq 1: [1, 464, 3797, 3332, 2] (no padding needed)
  • Seq 2: [PAD, 1, 15496, 995, 2] (padded on left)
Input tensor shape: (batch=2, seq_len=5)

Why LEFT padding? So the LAST token (most important for generation) is always at the same position!

Step 5: Create {term:attention-mask:Attention Mask}
  • Seq 1: [1, 1, 1, 1, 1] (all real tokens)
  • Seq 2: [0, 1, 1, 1, 1] (first is PAD, ignored)

Step 6: Create {term:causal-mask:Causal Mask} (Applied Internally)

For each sequence, lower triangular matrix:
pos0 pos1 pos2 pos3 pos4 pos0 [ 0, -∞, -∞, -∞, -∞ ] pos1 [ 0, 0, -∞, -∞, -∞ ] pos2 [ 0, 0, 0, -∞, -∞ ] pos3 [ 0, 0, 0, 0, -∞ ] pos4 [ 0, 0, 0, 0, 0 ]

This is combined with the attention mask for padding!

Step 7: Forward Pass → Output Shape
output = model(input_ids, attention_mask) output.shape = (batch=2, seq_len=5, vocab_size=50257)

At EACH position, the model outputs a probability distribution over the ENTIRE vocabulary!
  • For position 3 of Seq 1 ("sat"): P("on") = 0.15, P("down") = 0.12, P("EOS") = 0.08, ...

content.title: Step 8: Compute {term:loss:Loss} (Cross-Entropy)
content.content:
Labels (shifted ground truth):
  • Seq 1: [464, 3797, 3332, 2, -100] (-100 = ignore last position)
  • Seq 2: [-100, 15496, 995, 2, -100] (-100 for PAD positions)
Loss at each position: L = -log(P(correct_token))
  • If P("cat") = 0.85 at position 1: L = -log(0.85) = 0.16 (low = good!)
  • If P("cat") = 0.10 at position 1: L = -log(0.10) = 2.30 (high = bad!)
Total Loss = mean over all non-ignored positions

content.title: This is {term:teacher-forcing:Teacher Forcing}!
content.content: Notice: We process ALL positions in ONE forward pass using ground truth at each position. The {term:causal-mask:causal mask} ensures each position only 'sees' previous tokens. This is what makes transformer training so fast!

content.title: The Truth that gets Vague in Technical Jargon
content.content:
{term:pre-training:Pre-training}, {term:sft:SFT}, and Instruction Tuning use the EXACT SAME {term:loss:loss} function!

The computational mechanism is identical. The only difference is the {term:data:data} format and optionally which {term:token:tokens} contribute to the {term:loss:loss}.

explanation.template: For EACH {term:token:token}, compute the negative log {term:probability:probability} of predicting it correctly given all previous {term:token:tokens}. Sum across the sequence.

rows: Raw text chunks from books, web, code

content.title: For LLMs: EVERYTHING is Text Generation!
content.content:
TRAINING = prompt + answer as ONE sequence (one go, parallel in a batch):
  • Classification: Review: Great movie! Sentiment: positive
  • Translation: English: Hello → French: Bonjour
  • Question Answering: Capital of France? Answer: Paris
  • Code Generation: Write a function to add two numbers: def add(a, b): return a + b
No separate "target" text: it's the same sequence - training just predicts the next token everywhere (labels = input shifted by 1).

INFERENCE = send only what you have, model completes in a LOOP (sequential):
  • Send: Review: Great movie! Sentiment: - model generates: positive
  • Send: English: Hello → French: - model generates: Bonjour
SAME mechanism for ALL tasks!

Prompt Masking in {term:sft:SFT}:
  • Input: [Translate, :, Hello, →, Bon, jour]
  • Labels: [-100, -100, -100, -100, Bon, jour]
  • ↑ prompt (ignored) | ↑ response (trained)
Labels = -100 tells PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss to SKIP these positions. Loss only on response tokens!

content.title: The Core Difference: How Data and Output Look
content.content:
{term:encoder-only:Encoder-only} (BERT):
• Training {term:data:data} = (input, numeric_label) pairs
• Output = {term:probability:probability} vector from linear layer
• Example: 'I love this movie' → [0.02, 0.95, 0.03]

{term:decoder-only:Decoder-only} (LLM):
• Training {term:data:data} = FULL TEXT with answer included
• Output = generates the actual WORD as {term:token:tokens}
• Example: 'Sentiment: I love this movie → positive' (generates 'positive')

content.title: LLM Training: Input = TASK + PREDICTION, Labels = Shifted by 1
content.content:
During {term:sft:SFT}, the LLM sees the COMPLETE text including the answer. The input {term:token:tokens} are the full sequence, and the labels are the SAME sequence shifted by 1 position (standard next-{term:token:token} prediction).

Example:
  1. Full text: "Is this spam? 'Buy now!' Answer: spam"
  2. Input tokens: [Is, this, spam, ?, ', Buy, now, !', Answer, :, spam]
  3. Label tokens: [this, spam, ?, ', Buy, now, !', Answer, :, spam, {term:eos-token:EOS}]
The {term:model:model} learns to predict each next {term:token:token}. At inference, you stop at ':' and let it generate!

content.title: Key Insight: LLM Outputs are WORDS, Not Probabilities!
content.content:
The LLM doesn't output [0.95, 0.03, 0.02]. It generates the actual text!
  • Classification → generates 'positive' or 'negative'
  • Regression → generates '4' or '3.5' as text
  • {term:multi-label:Multi-label} → generates 'action, comedy, romance'
EVERYTHING is text generation!
{term:encoder-only:Encoder-only}: Losses and Equations

content.title: Multi-class vs Multi-label: The Critical Difference
content.content:
{term:multi-class:Multi-class} ({term:softmax:Softmax}): 'Out of ALL these, which ONE is it?'
→ {term:probability:Probabilities} sum to 1. Mutually exclusive.

{term:multi-label:Multi-label} ({term:sigmoid-activation:Sigmoid}): Ask each label INDEPENDENTLY:
  • 'Is it a car?' → 95% yes
  • 'Is it red?' → 87% yes
  • 'Is it German?' → 12% no
  • 'Is it sporty?' → 78% yes
Each output is its own yes/no decision - that's why we use {term:sigmoid-activation:Sigmoid}!

slides.title: 3 Tasks in ONE Batch: The Beauty of SFT

content.title: The Power of {term:sft:SFT}: Train on ANY mix of tasks in ONE batch!
content.content: With {term:sft:SFT}, you can throw Binary Classification, {term:multi-class:Multi-class}, {term:multi-label:Multi-label}, Regression, {term:ner:NER}, {term:extractive-qa:QA} - ALL in the SAME padded batch! The {term:model:model} learns from ALL of them together. That's the beauty of treating everything as text generation!

content.title: {term:encoder-only:Encoder-only}: Each task needs separate head
content.content:
Task 1 (Binary): {text: 'Congrats! You won!', label: 1}
Task 2 ({term:multi-class:Multi-class}): {text: 'Terrible movie', label: 1} (neg)
Task 3 ({term:multi-label:Multi-label}): {text: 'Action comedy', labels: [1,1,0,0]}

Each needs a DIFFERENT classification head. Can't mix in one batch easily!

content.title: LLM Training: 3 DIFFERENT tasks in ONE padded batch!
content.content:
Sample 1 (Binary - Spam):
  • Full text: "Is this spam? 'Congrats! You won!' Answer: spam"
  • Input: [Is, this, spam, ..., Answer, :, spam]
  • Labels: [this, spam, ..., Answer, :, spam, {term:eos-token:EOS}] (shifted by 1)
Sample 2 ({term:multi-class:Multi-class} - Sentiment):
  • Full text: "Sentiment: 'The movie was terrible' → negative"
  • Input/Labels: Same pattern - full text, shifted labels
Sample 3 ({term:multi-label:Multi-label} - Genre):
  • Full text: "List genres: 'A hilarious action movie' → action, comedy"
All 3 samples padded to same length, trained in ONE batch!

content.title: At Inference: Provide up to the trigger, let model generate
content.content:
Spam:
You give: "Is this spam? 'Buy pills cheap!' Answer:"
Model generates: "spam"

Sentiment:
You give: "Sentiment: 'I love this!' →"
Model generates: "positive"

Genre:
You give: "List genres: 'Scary thriller' →"
Model generates: "thriller, horror"

The {term:model:model} learned the PATTERN from training. With enough diverse {term:data:data}, it generalizes!
Training {term:data:Data} Format:

[ {"text": "Is this spam? 'Congrats! You won!' Answer: spam"}, {"text": "Sentiment: 'Movie was terrible' → negative"}, {"text": "List genres: 'Action comedy film' → action, comedy"}, {"text": "Rate 1-5: 'Great product!' → 5"} ]

content.title: Key Takeaway
content.content:
{term:encoder-only:Encoder-only}: Separate (input, label), different heads per task type

LLM ({term:sft:SFT}): ALL tasks as text completion in same batch, ONE {term:model:model} handles everything. The {term:model:model} generates the answer as {term:token:tokens}!

slides.title: Token Classification: Every Token Gets a Label

content.title: What is {term:token-classification:Token Classification}?
content.content:
Instead of ONE label for whole sequence, label EACH {term:token:token}:
  • {term:ner:NER}: John→B-PER, works→O, at→O, Google→B-ORG
  • {term:pos-tagging:POS}: John→NOUN, works→VERB, at→PREP
  • {term:extractive-qa:Extractive QA}: Each {term:token:token} → START/END/NONE

content.title: {term:encoder-only:Encoder-only} {term:ner:NER}: 2 batches, 5 labels
content.content:
Labels: [O, B-PER, I-PER, B-ORG, I-ORG]

Batch 1: tokens=['John','works','at','Google'], labels=[1,0,0,3]
Batch 2: tokens=['Elon','Musk','founded','Tesla'], labels=[1,2,0,3]

Processing:
  1. {term:hidden-state:Hidden states}: (batch=2, seq_len=4, hidden=768)
  2. Linear(768, 5) applied to EACH position
  3. Output: (batch=2, seq_len=4, num_labels=5)
  4. {term:loss:Loss}: CrossEntropy PER TOKEN, averaged

content.title: LLM: Again, EVERYTHING is text generation!
content.content:
For LLMs, {term:token-classification:token classification} becomes text completion. Train on full text with answer!

Same pattern as classification - input = FULL TEXT, labels = shifted by 1.

content.title: LLM Training: 3 Token Classification tasks in ONE batch
content.content:
Sample 1 ({term:ner:NER}):
"Extract entities: 'John works at Google' → [PER]John[/PER] works at [ORG]Google[/ORG]"

Sample 2 ({term:pos-tagging:POS}):
"POS tags: 'The quick fox' → The/DET quick/ADJ fox/NOUN"

Sample 3 ({term:extractive-qa:Extractive QA}):
"Context: 'Paris is capital of France' Q: 'What is capital?' A: Paris"

All padded, trained together!

content.title: Inference: Provide prompt, model generates annotations
content.content:
{term:ner:NER}:
You give: "Extract entities: 'Sundar works at Google' →"
Model generates: "[PER]Sundar[/PER] works at [ORG]Google[/ORG]"

{term:pos-tagging:POS}:
You give: "POS tags: 'Dogs run fast' →"
Model generates: "Dogs/NOUN run/VERB fast/ADV"

{term:extractive-qa:QA}:
You give: "Context: 'Berlin is in Germany' Q: 'Where is Berlin?' A:"
Model generates: "Germany"

content.title: Fill-in-the-Blank: Two Approaches
content.content:
Approach 1: {term:mask-token:[MASK]} Token ({term:encoder-only:Encoder-only})
Replace target with {term:mask-token:[MASK]}, {term:model:model} predicts from {term:vocabulary:vocabulary} at that position.

Approach 2: Generation ({term:decoder-only:Decoder-only})
Just complete the text! No special {term:token:token} needed - it's text generation!

content.title: {term:encoder-only:Encoder-only} {term:mask-token:[MASK]} Approach
content.content:
Input: 'The [MASK] of France is Paris'
Output shape: (batch, seq_len, vocab_size=30522)
At {term:mask-token:[MASK]} position: {term:logits:logits} over entire {term:vocabulary:vocabulary}

Top predictions:
  • capital: 0.85
  • city: 0.06
  • heart: 0.02

content.title: LLM: Just text generation!
content.content:
Training:
"Fill blank: 'The ___ of France is Paris' → capital"
Input: [Fill, blank, ..., →, capital]
Labels: [blank, ..., →, capital, {term:eos-token:EOS}]

Inference:
You give: "Fill blank: 'The ___ of France is Paris' →"
Model generates: "capital"

No {term:mask-token:[MASK]} {term:token:token} needed - just next-{term:token:token} prediction!

content.title: 🔬 [ADVANCED] Replacing the {term:lm-head:LM Head}
content.content: This is NOT the normal approach! But you CAN make a {term:decoder-only:decoder-only} LLM behave like an {term:encoder-only:encoder-only} {term:model:model} by replacing the {term:lm-head:LM head} with a custom classification/regression head.

content.title: Normal LLM vs Modified LLM
content.content:
Normal LLM (text generation):
{term:hidden-state:Hidden} (4096) → {term:lm-head:LM Head} (4096→32000) → Next {term:token:token} {term:logits:logits} → {term:vocabulary:Vocabulary} {term:probability:probabilities}

Modified LLM (classification):
{term:hidden-state:Hidden} (4096) → REMOVE {term:lm-head:LM Head} → Classification Head (4096→3) → Class {term:probability:probabilities}

This is NOT generation anymore! It's discriminative classification like {term:encoder-only:encoder-only}.

content.title: Why the LAST Token?
content.content:
Due to {term:causal-mask:causal attention}, only the LAST {term:token:token} has seen ALL previous {term:token:tokens}:
  • Position 0 sees: only position 0
  • Position 1 sees: positions 0-1
  • Position 2 sees: positions 0-2
  • ...
  • LAST {term:token:token} sees: ALL {term:token:tokens}!
So we extract last {term:token:token}'s {term:hidden-state:hidden state} and attach custom head. This is how HuggingFace's AutoModelForSequenceClassification works with {term:decoder-only:decoder} {term:model:models}!

content.title: When to Use Each Approach
content.content:
Use Text Generation (keep {term:lm-head:LM head}):
  • Zero-shot / few-shot scenarios
  • When you want reasoning in output
  • Training on mixed tasks easily
Use Custom Head (ADVANCED):
  • Fixed set of classes
  • Need exact {term:probability:probabilities}
  • Faster inference (no autoregressive)
  • HuggingFace AutoModelForSequenceClassification

slides.title: The Foundation: LLMs Only See Tokens

content.title: The Universal Truth About LLMs
content.content:
No matter the task - classification, QA, chat, code, translation - an LLM does exactly ONE thing:

See {term:token:tokens} → Predict next {term:token:token}.

That's it. EVERYTHING else is just clever formatting of the input text.

content.title: What Does the Model Actually See?
content.content:
You type: 'What is the capital of France?'

Model sees:
[1, 1824, 338, 278, 7483, 310, 3444, 29973]
(Just numbers! Token IDs from the {term:vocabulary:vocabulary})

Model outputs: A {term:probability:probability} distribution over ~50,000 possible next {term:token:tokens}

Top predictions:
{'Paris': 0.89, 'The': 0.03, 'France': 0.02, ...49997 others}

content.title: Every Task = Text Completion
content.content:
Classification: 'Sentiment: Great movie! → ' → generates 'positive'

Translation: 'English: Hello → French: ' → generates 'Bonjour'

Code: 'def add(a, b): ' → generates 'return a + b'

Chat: '[User] Hi! [Assistant] ' → generates 'Hello! How can I help?'

The ONLY difference between model types is HOW they were trained (what {term:data:data} format)!

Key Insight: Understanding this reveals why different training stages exist - they're all about teaching the {term:model:model} different patterns of input→output formatting, NOT different mechanisms.

content.title: What is a Base Model?
content.content:
A Base Model is the foundational LLM trained ONLY on next-{term:token:token} prediction from massive, unstructured text. It learns:

• Grammar & Syntax: How language is structured
• Semantics: What words mean and how they relate
• World Knowledge: Facts about entities, events, history
• Reasoning Patterns: Logical inference from statistical patterns

BUT it has NO concept of 'instructions' or 'responses'!

content.title: Training Data: What Does It Look Like?
content.content:
Sources:
• Web (Common Crawl, Wikipedia)
• Books (Project Gutenberg, BookCorpus)
• Code (GitHub, StackOverflow)
• Scientific papers (arXiv, PubMed)

Format: Just raw text chunks. No structure, no labels.
The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. Paris is the capital of France. The Eiffel Tower... def fibonacci(n): if n <= 1: return n return fibonacci(n-1) + fibonacci(n-2)

content.title: Step-by-Step: How Base Model Training Works
content.content:
Step 1: Take raw text: 'The cat sat on the mat'

Step 2: Create input-label pairs (shifted by 1):
Input: [{term:bos-token:BOS}, The, cat, sat, on, the, mat] Labels: [The, cat, sat, on, the, mat, {term:eos-token:EOS}]

Step 3: At each position, predict next {term:token:token}

Step 4: Compute {term:loss:loss}: How wrong was the prediction?
{term:loss:L} = −log {term:probability:P}(correct)

Step 5: Update {term:weights:weights} via {term:gradient:gradients}

Repeat for trillions of {term:token:tokens}!

slides.title: Instruction-Tuned Models: Learning to Follow Commands

content.title: What is an Instruction-Tuned Model?
content.content:
Take a base model, fine-tune it on (instruction, response) pairs, and now it UNDERSTANDS commands. Same {term:loss:loss} function, different {term:data:data}!

The {term:model:model} learns patterns like:
• 'When asked to translate, I should output the translation'
• 'When asked to summarize, I should be concise'
• 'After the instruction ends, I should respond'

content.title: Training Data: Instruction→Response Pairs
content.content:
Format:
{"instruction": "Translate to Spanish", "input": "Hello, how are you?", "output": "Hola, ¿cómo estás?"} {"instruction": "Summarize this text", "input": "Long article about climate change...", "output": "Climate change is accelerating due to..."} {"instruction": "Write a haiku about programming", "input": "", "output": "Code flows like water\nBugs appear then disappear\nShip it on Friday"}

content.title: Step-by-Step: How It's Trained
content.content:
Step 1: Format instruction-response pair as text:
Translate to French: Hello → Bonjour

Step 2: Full text becomes input, shifted by 1 for labels (just like base!)

Step 3: OPTIONAL but common: Mask prompt {term:token:tokens}
Input: [Translate, to, French, :, Hello, →, Bonjour] Labels: [-100, -100, -100, -100, -100, -100, Bonjour, {term:eos-token:EOS}]
↑ -100 = ignore in {term:loss:loss}

Step 4: {term:loss:loss} computed ONLY on response {term:token:tokens}!

Result: {term:model:Model} learns: 'After → generate the answer'

content.title: What is a Chat Model?
content.content:
A Chat model is trained on MULTI-TURN conversations with role markers (system, user, assistant). It learns:

• Turn-taking: When to speak vs when to wait
• Context accumulation: Remember ALL prior turns
• Role adherence: Follow {term:system-prompt:system prompt} consistently
• Conversation ending: Know when conversation is complete

content.title: Training Data: Multi-Turn Conversations
content.content:
Format (JSONL):
{"messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a math tutor."}, {"role": "user", "content": "What is 2+2?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "The answer is 4."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Now multiply by 10"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "4 × 10 = 40"} ]}

Key insight: The {term:model:model} sees the ENTIRE history at each turn!

content.title: The {term:chat-template:Chat Template}: How Turns Become Tokens
What is an RL-Aligned Model?
content.content:
An RL-aligned model goes BEYOND following instructions - it learns WHAT KIND of responses humans PREFER. This is Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).

Why? A {term:model:model} can follow instructions but still be:
• Verbose when brevity is wanted
• Harmful when asked dangerous things
• Sycophantic (just agreeing with user)
• Missing nuance in complex answers

RLHF teaches: 'Not just HOW to respond, but WHAT makes a GOOD response.'

content.title: Step-by-Step: The RLHF Pipeline
content.content:
Step 1: Collect {term:preference-data:Preference Data}
• Generate multiple responses per prompt
• Humans rank: 'A is better than B'

Step 2: Train {term:reward-model:Reward Model}
• Input: (prompt, response) → Output: score
• Learns to predict human preference
{term:reward:R}('Helpful answer') = 0.85 {term:reward:R}('Harmful answer') = -0.94

Step 3: Optimize {term:policy:Policy} (the LLM)
• Generate responses
• {term:reward-model:Reward model} scores them
• Update {term:weights:weights} to increase {term:reward:reward}
• {term:kl:KL} penalty prevents drifting too far from SFT

explanation.template: Maximize {term:reward:reward} from human preferences, but don't drift too far from the SFT {term:model:model} (controlled by {term:kl:KL} penalty).

content.title: {term:preference-data:Preference Data} Format
content.content:
{"prompt": "Explain gravity to a 5-year-old", "chosen": "Gravity is like invisible glue that...", "rejected": "Gravitational force is the curvature..."}

Why 'chosen' wins: Audience-appropriate, simple language

Training creates pairs: (prompt, A, B) where A is preferred

Alternatives to PPO:
• DPO (Direct Preference Optimization): Skip reward model, optimize directly on preferences
• GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization): Used by DeepSeek, more efficient

content.title: Reasoning Models: Same Architecture, Different Training
content.content:
Reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1, o1) are NOT architecturally different! They're trained to generate intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer.

What makes them 'reasoning' models:
• CoT Data Format: Training data includes <think> tags with step-by-step reasoning
• Verifiable Rewards: RL uses accuracy rewards (compiler checks, math verification) + format rewards (ensure reasoning in <think> tags)
• NOT human preference rewards - but deterministic verification!

3 ways to build reasoning models:
• Pure RL: RL directly on base model with verifiable rewards (DeepSeek-R1-Zero showed reasoning 'emerges'!)
• SFT + RL: {term:sft:SFT} on CoT data → RL with verifiable rewards (typical pipeline)
• Distillation: {term:sft:SFT} on CoT outputs from larger reasoning models

Key insight: The verbose, step-by-step responses you see? That's learned behavior from training data format + rewards, not a magical architecture change!
Read more about Reasoning models here

slides.title: The Evolution: From Raw to Refined

content.title: The Full Picture: What Changes, What Stays Same
content.content:
ALWAYS THE SAME:
• Architecture (Transformer decoder)
• Tokenizer ({term:vocabulary:vocabulary})
• Fundamental mechanism (next {term:token:token} prediction)
• {term:causal-mask:Causal attention} structure

WHAT CHANGES:
• Training {term:data:data} format
• {term:loss:loss} computation (which {term:token:tokens} count)
• Optimization objective (CE vs {term:reward:reward})
• Capabilities and behaviors

content.title: The Training Pipeline (Typical Modern LLM)
content.content:
Phase 1: {term:pre-training:Pre-training} (~months, $millions)
Random {term:weights:weights} → Train on trillions of {term:token:tokens} → Base Model

Phase 2: {term:sft:SFT} (~days, $thousands)
Base Model → Train on instruction {term:data:data} → Instruction Model

Phase 3: RLHF/DPO (~days, $thousands)
Instruction Model → Train on {term:preference-data:preferences} → RL-Aligned Model

Result: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, LLaMA-Chat, etc.

Key Takeaway: All these stages use the SAME architecture doing the SAME thing (predicting {term:token:tokens}). The magic is in how we format the training {term:data:data} to teach different behaviors!

slides.title: The Fine-tuning Spectrum: How Much to Train?

content.title: One Question, Many Answers
content.content:
When you want to adapt a pre-trained {term:model:model} for your task, you have choices:

• {term:full-finetuning:Full Fine-tuning}: Train EVERYTHING
• {term:partial-finetuning:Partial Fine-tuning}: Freeze some, train some
• {term:peft:PEFT}: Freeze all, add tiny {term:trainable-layer:trainable} modules

Which is best? It depends on your data, compute budget, and task!

content.title: These Techniques Work for ANY Deep Learning Model!
content.content:
While we're discussing LLMs, these approaches apply to:
  • Vision models: ResNet, ViT, CLIP
  • Encoder-only: BERT, RoBERTa, Sentence Transformers
  • Decoder-only: GPT, LLaMA, Mistral
  • Encoder-Decoder: T5, BART
  • Multimodal: LLaVA, Flamingo
The principles are universal! Freeze vs train, add adapters, low-rank decomposition - all work across architectures.
Key Question: How much of the {term:model:model}'s knowledge do you need to change? The answer guides your choice.

slides.title: Full Fine-tuning: Maximum Power, Maximum Cost

content.title: How {term:full-finetuning:Full Fine-tuning} Works
content.content:
Update ALL {term:weights:parameters} in the {term:model:model}:

for param in model.parameters(): param.requires_grad = True # Everything is trainable! # Standard training loop for batch in data: loss = model(batch) loss.backward() # Gradients for ALL 7B params optimizer.step() # Update ALL 7B params

content.title: Adding New Layers on Top
Step-by-Step: What Happens to Data
content.content:
Step 1: Input batch → Tokenized IDs
["Classify: Great movie!"] → [345, 2883, 32, 1893, 999]

Step 2: Forward pass through ALL layers (7B params active)
Input → Embeddings → 32 Transformer blocks → Hidden states

Step 3: Compute {term:loss:loss}
loss = CrossEntropy(logits, labels)

Step 4: Backward pass → {term:gradient:Gradients} for ALL 7B params!

Step 5: {term:weights:Weights} updated everywhere:
θ_new = θ_old - lr × ∇L # For all 7 billion params

content.title: When to Use {term:full-finetuning:Full Fine-tuning}
content.content:
• ✅ Large, diverse training dataset (100K+ examples)
  • ✅ Target domain is very different from pretraining
  • ✅ Maximum accuracy required (production systems)
  • ✅ Have the compute budget (multi-GPU, days of training)
  • ❌ Avoid if: Small dataset (risk of overfitting), limited compute

slides.title: Partial Fine-tuning: Freeze the Foundation, Train the Top

content.title: The Key Insight
content.content:
{term:partial-finetuning:Partial fine-tuning} freezes early layers (general language knowledge) and only trains later layers (task-specific adaptation). This is ALSO called a {term:peft:PEFT} technique!

Why it works: Research shows early layers learn general features (word meanings, syntax) while later layers learn task-specific patterns. For many tasks, you only need to adapt the 'top' of the model.

content.title: How to Freeze Layers
content.content:
# Freeze first 24 of 32 transformer layers for name, param in model.named_parameters(): # Freeze embeddings and early layers if 'embed' in name: param.requires_grad = False elif 'layers.' in name: layer_num = int(name.split('layers.')[1].split('.')[0]) if layer_num < 24: # Freeze layers 0-23 param.requires_grad = False else: param.requires_grad = True # Train layers 24-31 elif 'lm_head' in name: param.requires_grad = True # Train output layer # Count trainable vs frozen trainable = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad) total = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) print(f"Training {trainable/total:.1%} of parameters")

Output: Training 25.0% of parameters

content.title: Step-by-Step: Data Flow
content.content:
Step 1: Input passes through {term:frozen-layer:frozen} layers 0-23
• Forward pass: Normal computation
• Backward pass: No {term:gradient:gradient} computation (faster!)

Step 2: Input reaches {term:trainable-layer:trainable} layers 24-31
• Forward pass: Normal computation
• Backward pass: {term:gradient:Gradients} computed, {term:weights:weights} updated

Memory saved: Optimizer states only for trainable layers:
  • Full: 7B × 12 bytes = 84 GB optimizer states
  • Partial (25%): 1.75B × 12 bytes = 21 GB optimizer states

content.title: Adding New Layers + Freezing Base
content.content:
You can ALSO attach new layers while freezing the entire pretrained {term:model:model}:

# Freeze ENTIRE pretrained model for param in pretrained_model.parameters(): param.requires_grad = False # Add new trainable layers classifier = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(4096, 512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.1), nn.Linear(512, num_classes) ) # Only classifier is trainable!

This is like using the LLM as a powerful 'feature extractor' and training only your custom head.

rows: Still needs full model in memory
Choosing which layers is an art

content.title: When to Use {term:partial-finetuning:Partial Fine-tuning}
content.content:
• ✅ Medium-sized dataset (10K-100K examples)
  • ✅ Task is related to pretraining (e.g., sentiment from general LLM)
  • ✅ Want faster training than full fine-tuning
  • ✅ GPU memory is limited (can fit partial but not full)
  • ❌ Avoid if: Task requires fundamentally new patterns

content.title: What is {term:peft:Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning}?
content.content:
{term:peft:PEFT} methods keep the ENTIRE pretrained {term:model:model} {term:frozen-layer:frozen} and add tiny {term:trainable-layer:trainable} components. Train <1% of parameters, achieve 90-100% of full fine-tuning performance!

The insight: Weight updates during fine-tuning have low 'intrinsic dimensionality' - they can be represented efficiently in a much smaller space.

content.title: The PEFT Family Tree
content.content:
1. {term:prompt-tuning:Prompt Tuning}
• Add learnable vectors at INPUT only
• Fewest parameters (~10K)
• Simplest, works for simple tasks

2. {term:prefix-tuning:Prefix Tuning}
• Add learnable vectors to K/V in ALL attention layers
• More parameters (~100K-1M)
• Better for generation tasks

3. {term:adapter:Adapter Layers}
• Insert small networks between transformer layers
• Bottleneck architecture (project down, then up)
• Good but adds inference latency

4. {term:lora:LoRA} (Low-Rank Adaptation) ⭐
• Add low-rank matrices parallel to attention weights
• Most popular PEFT method today
• No inference latency (can merge weights)

content.title: Why LoRA Won
content.content:
{term:lora:LoRA} became the most popular because:
  • No inference overhead: Merge B·A back into W → same inference speed!
  • Simple implementation: Just add two matrices per layer
  • Flexible: Choose which layers to apply (usually attention Q, K, V)
  • Swappable: Load different LoRA adapters for different tasks
Next slide: Deep dive into how {term:lora:LoRA} works mathematically!

slides.title: LoRA Deep Dive: The Math Behind the Magic

content.title: The Core Idea
content.content:
Instead of updating a huge weight matrix W directly, {term:lora:LoRA} learns a 'delta' ΔW that can be represented as the product of two much smaller matrices:

Original: W ∈ ℝ^{d×k} (e.g., 4096×4096 = 16M params)
LoRA: ΔW = B·A where B ∈ ℝ^{d×{term:lora-rank:r}}, A ∈ ℝ^{{term:lora-rank:r}×k}

With {term:lora-rank:r}=8: (4096×8) + (8×4096) = 65,536 params → 99.6% reduction!

explanation.template: Output = {term:frozen-layer:frozen} pretrained portion + scaled {term:lora:LoRA} adaptation. The α/r scaling controls the 'strength' of the adaptation.

content.title: Step-by-Step: How LoRA Transforms Data
content.content:
Original Attention (no LoRA):
Q = x @ W_Q # x: (batch, seq, 4096), W_Q: (4096, 4096) # Q shape: (batch, seq, 4096)

With LoRA (r=8):
# Frozen pretrained path Q_frozen = x @ W_Q # (batch, seq, 4096) # LoRA adaptation path x_proj = x @ A # A: (4096, 8) → (batch, seq, 8) Q_lora = x_proj @ B # B: (8, 4096) → (batch, seq, 4096) # Combined output Q = Q_frozen + (α/r) * Q_lora # Same shape: (batch, seq, 4096)

Training: Only A and B receive {term:gradient:gradients}. W_Q stays {term:frozen-layer:frozen}!

content.title: Initialization Matters!
content.content:
Matrix A: Initialized from Gaussian, scaled by 1/√r
Matrix B: Initialized to ZEROS

Why? At the start of training, ΔW = B·A = 0 → The model starts exactly as the pretrained model! No 'shock' to the model at beginning of training.

# From typical implementation scaling_factor = 1 / np.sqrt(rank) A = np.random.randn(input_dim, rank) * scaling_factor B = np.zeros((rank, output_dim)) # Starts at zero!

Result: Initial output = W₀·x + 0 = pretrained behavior. Training gradually adapts.

content.title: After Training: Merge for Zero Latency
content.content:
Once trained, you can merge {term:lora:LoRA} back into the original weights:

# During inference, merge LoRA into original weights W_merged = W_Q + (α/r) * B @ A # Now use W_merged like normal - no extra computation! Q = x @ W_merged

Result: Same inference speed as original model, but with fine-tuned behavior!

content.title: Decision Flowchart
content.content:
1. How much data do you have?
• <1K examples: Use {term:lora:LoRA} (prevents overfitting)
• 1K-100K examples: {term:lora:LoRA} or {term:partial-finetuning:partial fine-tuning}
• >100K examples: Consider {term:full-finetuning:full fine-tuning}

2. How different is your domain?
• Similar to pretraining: {term:lora:LoRA} is usually enough
• Very different domain: {term:full-finetuning:Full fine-tuning} may be needed

3. What's your compute budget?
• Single consumer GPU (16-24GB): {term:lora:LoRA} only option
• Multi-GPU (80GB+): Any approach works

content.title: Practical LoRA Configuration (Recommended Defaults)
content.content: from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model config = LoraConfig( r=16, # Rank (start here, increase if needed) lora_alpha=32, # Scaling factor (2×r is common) target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj"], lora_dropout=0.05, # Small dropout for regularization bias="none", # Usually don't train biases task_type="CAUSAL_LM" ) model = get_peft_model(base_model, config) model.print_trainable_parameters() # Output: "trainable params: 4,194,304 || all params: 6,742,609,920 || trainable%: 0.0622"

content.title: Key Takeaways
content.content:
1. Start with LoRA: It's the default choice for most fine-tuning tasks today

2. Rank matters: r=8-16 for simple tasks, r=32-64 for complex domains

3. Full fine-tuning is rare: Most practitioners use PEFT unless they have massive datasets and compute

4. You can stack: LoRA on top of partially frozen model for maximum control

5. Experiment: The 'optimal' approach varies by task - always validate on held-out data!
